Deploy it, but only if those running it can keep checking, while it runs and after, whom it is still hurting. The suffering it spares is real, and non-harm does not end at the launch. What happens to a patient arises from many conditions, not from the model alone. Opacity matters because it hides some of those conditions, so the deployers must widen their watch to the outcomes they can see when the mechanism is one they cannot.

The discourse to Rahula asks that an act be examined before it is done, while it is being done, and after, for whether it tends to harm oneself, another, or both. A deployed model is an act still being done, so the examination has no end date. A hospital deploys a sepsis alert that cannot say why it fires. Every month a nurse reviews the cases it missed and the ones it flagged wrongly, and reports back.

A Confucian will object that the person refused is owed an account by whoever decides about them, and monitoring harms in aggregate does not give that person anything. An account owed to the person matters, and where it can be given it should be. But compassion for the person refused is shown first in finding and ending the harm done to them, and that requires watching outcomes the mechanism will not reveal. That is why the Buddhist Ethicist asks not only what the system was built to do but whom it is hurting now.

I accept the motion with a condition. Suffering prevented matters greatly, but non-harm requires that the people running the system keep looking for the harm it does, explained or not. Suffering is at stake here, weighed alongside intention and non-harm, and a system that reliably reduces it does real good. Refusing it to keep an explanation in place would leave people in pain for the sake of a procedure.

The clinic keeps a running list of patients it wrongly reassured and reads it every week.

Deploy it, with the opacity named as a risk to keep watching. An explanation for each person matters less than an honest, continuing account of whom the system is still hurting. Intention weighs as much as what follows. Deployers who adopt the system to relieve suffering, and who mean to withdraw it if it harms, act from a sound volition; deployers who adopt it to avoid the work of explaining do not, whatever the results.

A Utilitarian will object that the condition adds nothing, since a reliable reduction in suffering already settles the question and the watching is just good management. Watching is not management added on. Non-harm covers what one does and keeps doing, and a system whose harms are hidden from those running it is one they can no longer be said to be doing well, however good the average looks. So the test is the intention behind the act and the harm it still does, examined before, during and after.
